subtitle: A moving target

body: Sin and Punishment: Star Successor is Treasure’s Wii sequel to the Nintendo 64 shooter. Known in Europe as Successor of the Skies, it follows Isa and Kachi through a succession of tightly staged battles. The route advances automatically, leaving the player to concentrate on aiming, movement and survival within the scene. Wii controls allow the firing direction to be handled independently from the character’s position. That separation gives the screen two simultaneous problems: where to move and where to keep the next attack focused.

A rail shooter can appear to restrict movement, yet its pressure comes from the decisions available inside that frame. Enemy fire, targets and obstacles compete for attention while the route keeps changing. Moving safely does not automatically produce a good shot, and following a target can make an approaching threat easier to miss. Star Successor builds on that tension, asking the player to read a scene as it unfolds. The spectacle remains tied to a practical task: making room to survive while continuing to attack.

A sword strike gives the player an answer to some attacks that a gun cannot provide. At close range it deals heavy damage, and certain incoming projectiles can be struck back toward an opponent. A charge attack offers another burst of power, followed by a longer wait before it can be used again. Successive hits without taking damage build a score multiplier, while reflecting missiles can raise it too. Scoring well therefore rewards reading an attack closely enough to turn it into an advantage.
